steps.title: "Who," "which," "that" — but only sometimes
body: الَّذِي (masculine) and الَّتِي (feminine) both mean "who / which / that," and they join a description onto a noun: الرَّجُلُ الَّذِي سَافَرَ إِلَى الْمَدِينَةِ — "the man who traveled to the city." They agree with the noun they describe, not with anything in the description itself.

The one rule that matters most: الَّذِي/الَّتِي only appear after a DEFINITE noun — one with الـ. Take the الـ away, and the relative pronoun disappears completely, not just its own الـ: رَأَيْتُ طَالِبًا يَدْرُسُ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ — "I saw a student who studies Arabic" has no الَّذِي anywhere, because طَالِبًا is indefinite.

This lesson only covers the simplest shape: the noun being described is also the one doing the action in the description (الرَّجُلُ... سَافَرَ — the man is the one who traveled). Descriptions where the noun is instead the *object* ("the book that I read") need one more piece — a pronoun suffix pointing back to it — and that's its own lesson, later.

steps.title: Four relative clauses
steps.intro: Read each sentence, then check whether it uses الَّذِي, الَّتِي, or no relative pronoun at all. Tap 🔊 to hear any line.

steps.title: Definite needs a pronoun
steps.prompt: الرَّجُلُ (the man) is definite. Which word must follow it to start the description?

options.label: Nothing — descriptions never need a linking word

steps.explanation: الرَّجُلُ is masculine and definite, so الَّذِي is required before the description that follows.

steps.title: Indefinite needs nothing
steps.prompt: طَالِبًا (a student) is indefinite. What comes right before يَدْرُسُ (studies)?

options.label: Nothing — the description just follows directly

steps.explanation: Because طَالِبًا has no الـ, no relative pronoun appears at all — this is the single most common mistake to watch for in the other direction.

steps.title: Agreement follows the noun
steps.prompt: Why is it الَّتِي here, and not الَّذِي?

options.label: الْمَرْأَةُ (the woman) is feminine, and الَّتِي agrees with the antecedent, not the verb
تَتَكَلَّمُ (she speaks) happens to be a feminine-sounding verb

steps.explanation: الَّذِي/الَّتِي always match the gender of the noun being described — here that's الْمَرْأَةُ, feminine, so الَّتِي.

steps.title: You can build your first relative clauses
steps.message: Definite noun + الَّذِي/الَّتِي + a clause describing it, or indefinite noun + the clause with no pronoun at all — the two shapes that cover most everyday descriptions. Descriptions of an object ("the book that I read") are still ahead.
